vignette:
Omar, a man of 78 years with hands calloused from decades of roofing, first encountered the insidious grip of fear during a large industrial job three years ago. He was applying new insulation on the sprawling roof of a factory complex when, without warning, a faulty valve on an adjacent section burst, releasing a thick, acrid cloud that enveloped his work area. He remembered the sudden burning in his eyes and throat, the metallic taste that coated his tongue, and the desperate scramble for fresh air. In the days that followed, the true horror began to unfold in local news reports: the chemical was highly toxic, and the plume had drifted directly over a nearby elementary school during recess. Though officials initially downplayed immediate danger, the long-term health implications for children were widely discussed, painting a stark picture of potential irreversible harm.

In the aftermath, Omar found that when he tried to deliberately remember the sequence of events from that day - the exact moment the valve burst, the faces of his colleagues, the specific sensations - he found it difficult to access the memory. It felt fragmented, elusive, just beyond his conscious grasp. Yet, paradoxically, the memory would force its way into his mind without warning, often when he was trying to focus on something else entirely, an unwelcome intrusion that stole his peace. Sometimes, he would be overcome by the full emotional intensity of the event - the terror, the guilt, the crushing sense of helplessness - without any clear image or specific memory flashing before his eyes. It was a disembodied dread that left him breathless and disoriented.

The world slowly became a landscape of hidden threats for Omar. He found himself unable to relax, even when he knew he was in the safe confines of his own home. His body remained perpetually tensed, his mind scanning for dangers that weren't there. His wife, Aisha, noticed his increasing jumpiness; he would react with alarm when she touched him unexpectedly, a gentle hand on his shoulder sending a jolt of panic through him. Sleep, once a reliable comfort, became an elusive struggle. He would lie awake for hours, his mind replaying fragments of the incident or simply buzzing with an unshakeable sense of dread, making it difficult to fall or stay asleep.

The presence of children now brought a profound unease. Walking past a park, hearing the distant sound of children playing, or even seeing a child's drawing taped to a window would trigger a wave of nausea and a tightening in his chest. He had come to believe that he might be somehow responsible, or that the world was simply too dangerous for innocence, a conviction rooted in the memory of the news reports about the elementary school. He began to actively avoid places where children might gather, making excuses to Aisha when she suggested visiting their grandchildren. Similarly, any related news, even a general report about industrial accidents or environmental contamination, would send a jolt of anxiety through him, prompting him to immediately turn off the television or put down the newspaper. He was certain that such reports only served to confirm his worst fears about the world. Encountering known people from that time, particularly former colleagues who were also on the job site or even just seeing someone who resembled a local official he remembered from the news briefings, could trigger a sudden flash of intense anxiety, pulling him back to the moment of exposure or the subsequent dread.

Omar's once meticulous work as a roofer began to suffer. His chronic sleep problems meant his hands sometimes trembled, and his focus wavered, making him more prone to miscalculations on dangerous heights. He started turning down jobs in residential areas, especially those near schools, fabricating excuses about his age or busy schedule. He couldn't bear the thought of working so close to children, convinced he might somehow be a vector of residual harm, or that another disaster might strike. This significantly impacted his income and his deep pride in his craft, as he had always been a reliable and sought-after professional. Aisha, his wife of fifty years, had watched her vibrant husband recede into himself, his laughter less frequent, his eyes holding a perpetual wariness. It was her quiet, persistent concern, coupled with the profound loneliness he felt in his own home, that finally brought Omar to seek help, desperately hoping to reclaim some semblance of the peace he had lost.
